title: America Is Rediscovering Whole Grain Flour. Indian Families Have Been Grinding Their Own Atta for Generations.
excerpt: The craft flour movement sweeping Brooklyn bakeries and MAHA influencer feeds has a familiar parallel in every Indian kitchen that still uses a chakki.
body:
America is falling in love with flour again — but not the bleached, ultra-processed, shelf-stable kind that has dominated grocery aisles for decades. A new generation of consumers is paying $18 for a five-pound bag of stone-milled heritage wheat, and the movement is growing fast enough that one craft mill is building a $55 million facility to keep up with demand.

If you grew up in an Indian household, this might sound like a Tuesday.

## The Craft Flour Boom

Cairnspring Mills, a Washington State craft flour producer that supplies cult bakeries like California's Tartine and Phoenix's Pizzeria Bianco, saw revenue grow 51 per cent between 2023 and 2025. The company operates at a 41 per cent gross profit margin and is now building a new mill on land owned by the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation near Pendleton, Oregon. The Blue Mountain Mill will be capable of producing 110 million pounds of flour a year, up from eight million at Cairnspring's current facility.

The $55 million project, financed through a $35 million construction loan from Steward, a commercial lending platform for regenerative agriculture, plus equity investments from the Umatilla tribes and Mission Driven Finance, represents a bet that Americans are permanently changing how they think about grain.

Kevin Morse, Cairnspring's co-founder and CEO, wants to "do for flour what Blue Bottle did for coffee" — create a premium but accessible tier in a category that has a few industrial giants at the top and a sea of tiny independents at the bottom.

## Why Now

Several forces are converging. Fiber-maxxers, GLP-1 medication users adjusting their diets, and adherents of the Make America Healthy Again lifestyle are all seeking less processed, more nutritionally dense food. Big brands are scrambling to respond — PepsiCo has launched fiber-branded Sun Chips, Jell-O announced a new line without synthetic colours or artificial sweeteners, and restaurant chains are removing seed oils from their kitchens.

But for premium bakers, the shift is simpler. "Nothing weird added," says Craig Hutchinson, owner of Olmo, an upscale bagel shop in New Haven, Connecticut, that uses 82 per cent high-extraction flour milled from whole grain. Many customers report the bagels are easier to digest than conventional alternatives. High-extraction flour retains more grain structure than standard white flour because only a small percentage of the bran is sifted out.

When Mintel, the market research firm, asked consumers what would make them more likely to buy packaged bread, "premium flour" was the top choice among millennials and Gen Z — ahead of added protein, organic certification, and seasonal flavours.

## The Chakki Connection

For millions of Indian families, this is not new. The chakki — a traditional stone grinding mill — has been a fixture in Indian kitchens and neighbourhood flour mills for centuries. Fresh-ground atta retains the bran, germ, and endosperm of the wheat kernel, producing a flour that is nutritionally dense, high in fibre, and easier to digest than industrially processed alternatives.

Walk into any Indian grocery store in the United States and you will find brands like Sujata, Sharbati, and Aashirvaad selling stone-ground whole wheat flour that is functionally identical to what American craft mills are now marketing as a premium product. The difference is that a 20-pound bag of chakki atta costs roughly $12 at an Indian grocery, while the equivalent weight of craft flour can run $70 or more.

The irony is not lost on diaspora families watching Brooklyn sourdough enthusiasts discover that whole grain flour tastes better and digests easier. Indian cooking — rotis, parathas, puris — was always built around the assumption that flour should be whole, fresh, and minimally processed. The American food system stripped that out in the name of shelf life and uniformity. Now it is paying a premium to put it back.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The craft flour movement validates what many NRI families already practise. It also opens a commercial opportunity. Indian-American entrepreneurs with deep knowledge of grain milling traditions — from chakki mechanics to regional wheat varieties like sharbati and lokwan — are positioned to bridge the gap between artisanal American baking and South Asian grain wisdom.

Several Indian flour brands are already expanding their retail footprint in mainstream American grocery chains. As consumer demand for whole grain, heritage, and stone-milled products grows, the category could become a meaningful crossover point between Indian culinary tradition and American wellness culture.

The movement also has implications for Indian agriculture. India is the world's second-largest wheat producer, and its diverse wheat varieties, adapted to specific climates and soils, represent a genetic library that craft millers are only beginning to explore.

Bryan Ford, co-owner of Diljān bakery in Brooklyn and a Netflix and HBO host, put it simply: "The new currency moving forward is going to be, what's real? What's been manipulated the least?"

Indian grandmothers have been answering that question for a long time.
author: Diaspora Desk
